tasks.q: Ask the user for a title. Write a procedure called signoff that prints end of report, then display [title] and call signoff, so the title comes first.
brief: signoff takes nothing, prints that one line, and is called once.

tests.why: The title is printed first, then the procedure prints the sign-off. If you only see one line you have defined signoff but never called it - defining a procedure does not run it.
A different title, the same sign-off. If this failed you may have typed the title into the procedure instead of reading it with input().
The sign-off wording never changes, so it belongs inside the procedure. Printing it twice means you called signoff twice.

tasks.fb: A procedure is a named block of code you can run whenever you like. Writing def signoff(): only creates it - the line signoff() is what runs it.

teach.say: def gives a block of code a name. The indented lines do nothing until a line calls that name.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two headings, one on each line. Write a procedure called rule that prints =====, then display the rule, the first heading, the rule, the second heading and the rule, one on each line.
brief: Five lines in all, printed by one procedure called three times.

tests.why: There is a rule above, between and below the two headings, so rule() is called three times.
Different headings, same layout. If the headings came out in the wrong order, check you stored the first input() before reading the second.
Exactly five equals signs each time. Four or six will not match, and a rule printed inside the heading line will not either.

tasks.fb: The point of a procedure is that the code for the rule is written once. If you copied print('=====') out three times you have not used a subprogram at all.

tasks.q: Ask the user for two item names, one on each line. Write a procedure called label that takes one word and prints item: [word]. Call it once for each name, in the order they were typed.
brief: Nothing but those two lines is printed.

tests.why: The parameter is what makes one procedure work for both items. If both lines say the same word, you printed the same variable twice instead of passing each one in.
Nothing about the item is written inside the procedure - it arrives as the parameter.
The same word twice should print twice. If only one line appeared you may have skipped the second call, or only read one line of input.

tasks.fb: A parameter is the name the procedure gives to whatever is handed to it. The value you pass in when you call it is the argument.

teach.say: A parameter is a name in the brackets of the def line. Whatever you pass in when you call it arrives under that name.

tasks.q: Ask the user for the number of packs and then the price of one pack in pence. Write a procedure called charge that takes both and prints total [packs times price]. Call it, and print nothing else.
brief: Both are whole numbers, and the procedure does the printing.

tests.why: 4 packs at 75 pence is 300. If you got total 475 you joined the two inputs as text instead of turning them into numbers with int().
One pack costs the price of one pack. A multiplication that gives 99 only here but fails elsewhere usually means the arguments were passed the wrong way round.
Zero packs cost nothing, and the procedure still has to print a line. Printing nothing at all for this case is a common slip.
Bigger numbers must work too. If this failed but the others passed, you may have typed a fixed answer into the procedure.

tasks.fb: Two parameters are separated by a comma in the def line, and the arguments go in the same order when you call it. Order matters, not the names.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Write a function called double that returns twice its parameter and prints nothing at all, then display [what double hands back] and nothing else.
brief: The number may be negative or zero.
tasks.starter: # double returns, it does not print

tests.why: Double 7 is 14. If nothing was printed, your function returns the answer but the main program never printed it.
Double zero is zero, and it still has to be printed.
Negative numbers double too. If you used a loop that adds, it may not run for a negative value.
If this one failed, check you used int(input()) - doubling the text '250' gives 250250.

tasks.fb: return hands a value back to whatever called the function, so print(double(7)) prints 14. Without return the function hands back None.

teach.say: return hands a value back to the line that called the function, so the caller is the one that prints or stores it.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a width and then a height, both whole numbers. Write a function called area that returns width times height and holds no print at all. Store what it returns and display one line, area [that value].
brief: A single space goes after area, and nothing else is printed.
tasks.starter: # store the returned value before printing it

tests.why: One line only. If you got an extra line with 20 on its own, your function printed the answer as well as returning it - that is the mistake this question is about.
A one by one rectangle has area 1. If the line read area None, the function printed the answer instead of returning it, so there was nothing to hand back.
A height of 0 gives an area of 0, and the line must still be printed.
If only the first test passed, you may have written the answer into the function rather than calculating it from the parameters.

tasks.fb: Printing and returning are not the same thing. A function that prints shows the value once and throws it away; a function that returns gives it to the caller, which can store it, add to it or print it.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a name and then a whole number mark. Write a function called grade that returns pass for a mark of 40 or more and fail below 40, and a procedure called report that displays [name]: [that word].
brief: Use both subprograms, and print one line only.
tasks.starter: # grade returns a word, report prints the line

tests.why: 55 is a pass, and the procedure does the printing. Two lines of output means grade printed as well as returned.
Exactly 40 is a pass. Getting fail here means you tested mark > 40 instead of mark >= 40.
39 is under 40. If this printed pass, your function may be returning a value only on the pass branch and None otherwise.
A mark of 0 is still a mark and must be reported. Crashing here usually means int() was never used on the second input.

tasks.fb: OCR asks for the difference by name: a function returns a value, a procedure does not. In this program grade is the function and report is the procedure, and the program needs both.

teach.say: A function ends with return and hands a value back; a procedure only prints. So a function's answer can be passed straight into a procedure.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a whole number and keep it in a variable called total. Write a procedure called boost with a local total of its own, set to 99, that prints it. Call boost, then display [the main total].
brief: Two lines, the 99 first. The main program's total must not change.

tests.why: The 5 survives. If the second line also says 99, you wrote global total inside the procedure, so it changed the main program's variable instead of making a local one.
Zero is still the main program's value afterwards.
If this crashed, check you used int(input()) - a minus sign is fine for int but not for a text comparison.
If the second line printed 99 only on some tests, the procedure is printing after the main program rather than before. Call boost first, then print.

tasks.fb: A variable created inside a subprogram is local: it exists only while the subprogram runs and disappears afterwards. The main program's total is a different variable that happens to share a name.

teach.say: A name given a value inside a subprogram is local and vanishes when the subprogram ends. To change a variable from outside instead, the subprogram must say global first.

tasks.q: Write a procedure called win that adds 3 to a shared score and a procedure called draw that adds 1. Ask the user for the number of rounds, call win and then draw once per round, and display [the final score].
brief: The score starts at 0, fixed in the program and shared by the whole program, not typed in.
tasks.starter: # win and draw change the main program's score

tests.why: No rounds, so nothing is added and the starting score is printed. A program that prints something else here never handled the loop running zero times.
One round is 3 plus 1. If you got 0, the procedures made their own local score instead of changing the main program's - they need global score.
Five rounds at 4 each is 20. Getting 4 means the score is being reset to 0 somewhere inside the loop or inside a procedure.
If this gave 15 or 9, only one of the two procedures is being called inside the loop.

tasks.fb: A global variable is one the whole program can see. A subprogram may read it without saying anything, but to change it the subprogram must declare global first, or Python makes a local copy instead.

tasks.q: Write a function called points that returns 3 for 2 or more goals, 1 for one goal and 0 for none. Ask the user for the number of matches, then that many goal counts, one on each line. Display [the points added up].
brief: Call points once per match, inside the loop, and print only that one total.
tasks.starter: # one call per match, added to a running total

tests.why: 3 plus 1 plus 0 is 4. If you got 3, the total is being replaced each time round the loop instead of added to.
Five goals is still just 3 points, because the function returns 3 for anything from 2 upwards.
No matches at all, so the loop never runs and the total is still 0. The program must still print a line. Crashing here means you read a goals line before checking how many matches there were.
Two draws and two losses is 2. If this crashed with an input error, your loop is reading more lines than there are matches.
Two wins is 6. If the total came out as 3, the function is being called once outside the loop rather than once per match.

tasks.fb: Calling a subprogram inside a loop is how one piece of code gets reused on every item. The loop deals with how many times; the function deals with one match at a time.

teach.say: What a function returns is an ordinary value, so it can be added up. Called inside a loop, it runs once per turn.

tasks.q: Ask the user for a number of nights and then a number of guests. Display nights [the number of nights], then total [the total cost] on the next line.
brief: Write a function fee that returns nights times 25, and a function total that calls fee and returns fee times guests, plus 10.
Write a procedure receipt that calls total and prints both lines.
tasks.starter: # receipt calls total, total calls fee

tests.why: 2 nights is a fee of 50, times 3 guests is 150, plus 10 is 160. Getting 60 means the 10 was added before multiplying by the guests.
25 for one night, times one guest, plus 10. If the second line said total None, total prints instead of returning, so receipt had nothing to print.
No nights still costs the 10 booking charge. A program that skips the whole calculation when nights is 0 will print the wrong thing here.
125 for the nights, times 2 guests, plus 10. If this failed, check total is calling fee rather than repeating the times 25 itself.

tasks.fb: Subprograms can call subprograms. receipt calls total, total calls fee, and each one only has to know its own job - that is how a big program is broken into small ones.

tasks.q: Is each subprogram a function or a procedure?
items: Works out an area and returns it
Returns pass or fail for a mark
Returns the total of a list
tasks.fb: If a value comes back it is a function. If it only does a job, it is a procedure.

info.title: Why bother
info.text: A job written once and called from four places is tested once and fixed once. The same lines copied four times are four bugs waiting to happen.

info.title: Default values
info.text: A parameter can be given a default, so label("Juice") still works when the price is usually the same.

info.title: Returning more
info.text: return can hand back several values at once, separated by commas, and the caller unpacks them.

info.title: Already written
info.text: len(), int() and round() are functions somebody else wrote: you call them exactly the way you call your own.

info.title: Globals are risky
info.text: Any subprogram can change a global, so one bug can break all of them. Parameters and return values are safer.

info.title: Calling itself
info.text: A subprogram is even allowed to call itself. That is called recursion, and it is how a merge sort splits a list.
